droppedAtVerification.name: ML Visualiser
droppedAtVerification.why: Biggest time sink: the XOR demo effectively never finishes in a study session. The speed slider maxes at 20, and the loop is setTimeout(1000/speed) per *single* training example with 4 examples per epoch — so 5 epochs/sec is the ceiling. I reimplemented the site's exact update rule (lr hardcoded at 0.1, 2-4-1 sigmoid, online SGD) and ran 8 random seeds: convergence to its own <0.05 threshold takes 7,668–10,413 epochs, i.e. 26–35 minutes of staring at the tab. Worse, the error sits on the sigmoid plateau nearly motionless for the first stretch — seed 0 reads mean|error| 0.4997 at 1 min, 0.4972 at 5 min, 0.4354 at 10 min, and only reaches 0.0589 at 30 min. Most learners will watch "Current Error: 0.49" not budge and conclude the page is broken. Because it is setTimeout-driven it is also subject to background-tab throttling (~1 Hz), which stretches convergence to roughly ten hours if you switch tabs. Second: the CNN module is actively miseducating rather than merely thin — you will believe you watched a CNN classify a digit when it read the label. It also offers only 10 pre-baked digit samples with no drawing (zero onMouseDown/onMouseEnter handlers) and no upload, so you cannot probe it with an ambiguous input, which is exactly the experiment that would expose the fake. Third: adding points on the decision-boundary page silently does nothing to the SVM and logistic boundaries. Minor: a React #418 hydration mismatch fires on load (theme toggle, non-fatal). No repo, no author, no license, so nothing is auditable from the outside and nothing will get fixed.

droppedAtVerification.name: AttentionViz
droppedAtVerification.why: Broken as listed — the interactive demo never renders data in any modern browser because the HTTPS frontend calls a plain-HTTP backend at a bare IP (18.219.70.154:8500). The site's own HSTS header (max-age=31556952) closes off the http:// workaround permanently once you have loaded the page once, so "just use http" is not a durable fix. The data backend is an unmanaged EC2 box with no TLS and no domain name; it is one instance-stop away from the project being fully dead, and it already serves a 68 MB blob in ~10s per model, so even a working session is slow (the app itself warns it "requires many megabytes and may take up to a minute to render"). Models are fixed and pre-computed (BERT, GPT-2, ViT) — no custom text, no custom images, no model upload. It is a 2023 VIS paper artifact, so the models are pre-LLM-era; the mechanistic ideas (induction heads, head specialisation) transferred to modern interpretability work but the specific models did not. Self-hosting depends on a Google Drive link that is outside the repo and could rot independently.

claimsInaccurate.name: ML Visualized
claimsInaccurate.correction: Two of the three named topics are real; the headline one is fabricated. (1) There are no diffusion models on this site at all. Grepping the site's own search index returns 0 hits for "diffusion", "transformer", "attention", "convolution", "CNN", "recurrent", "LSTM", "dropout" and "batchnorm". Deep learning stops at a 3-layer tanh MLP and an MNIST autoencoder. (2) "Full ML textbook" is overstated: it is 12 notebooks in 4 chapters. There is no decision tree, random forest, boosting, SVM, or naive Bayes notebook — Naive Bayes exists only as an outbound link to the author's UMD lecture-notes PDF, not as content. (3) "Every algorithm is animated" is nearly true but misleading about the kind of animation: 9 of the 12 pages animate via pre-rendered matplotlib/celluloid GIFs baked into the notebook output (you cannot change a parameter and re-run). Only 3 pages — Interactive Linear Regression, Interactive Perceptron, Interactive Logistic Regression — are live, and their interactivity is two sliders each (slope w and intercept b for linear regression), not general parameter control. Gradient descent and backprop, however, are accurately described and are the strongest material here.

claimsInaccurate.name: ML Visualiser
claimsInaccurate.correction: Only the neural-network module does what the list implies. Four specific corrections. (1) "Visualize NN architecture" — you can only view it, not build it. The network is hardcoded to [2,4,1] and the learning rate is hardcoded to 0.1; the only control is an animation-speed slider. Copies of this description circulating elsewhere add "with customizable architecture" — that is flatly false. (2) "watch signals propagate" is the one accurate part: real sigmoid forward pass, real backprop, neuron brightness = activation, green/red edges = weight sign. (3) "linear regression" — the site's own homepage card promises "interactive gradient descent animation" and there is no gradient descent in the app. It solves closed-form OLS (`slope=(nΣxy−ΣxΣy)/(nΣx²−(Σx)²)`) instantly. The "Animate BFL" button builds 20 frames by linearly interpolating (slope, intercept) from (−2,−5) to (2×slope_OLS, 2×intercept_OLS), then calls `.sort((a,b)=>b.error−a.error)` so the frames merely replay in descending-error order and look like optimization. It is a cosmetic sweep, not a descent trajectory. (4) "classification" — of the three algorithms, only KNN is actually implemented (euclidean distance, k nearest, majority vote). The "SVM" is just `w1*x+w2*y+b>=0` with w1/w2/b that you set by hand — no margin, no support vectors, no fitting. "Logistic Regression (Polynomial)" evaluates a sigmoid over polynomial features using a hardcoded weight vector [0,1,1,0,0,0,0] that is never fit. Consequence: if you add data points, the SVM and logistic boundaries do not move at all; only KNN's responds. Its "Animate Boundary" just sweeps w1=cos(θ), w2=sin(θ). (5) "CNN" is the most overstated. Conv and max-pool are real, but the 84-neuron fully-connected layer is decorative — `fc[i] = flat[i % 25] * (0.5 + 0.5*Math.random())` — and the digit prediction reads the sample's ground-truth label and assigns it 70–90%. It appears to classify perfectly because it is told the answer. There is no trained model and no MNIST inference.

claimsInaccurate.name: The Illustrated Transformer
claimsInaccurate.correction: "Gold-standard blog post explaining transformers" is fully accurate — it is live, complete, still cited by Stanford/Harvard/MIT/Princeton/CMU courses, and translated into 12 languages. But "hand-drawn visuals" is wrong. The 39 figures are clean digitally-drawn vector diagrams: colour-coded rectangle grids for vectors, sans-serif labels, uniform pastel fills (green embeddings, purple queries, orange keys, blue values). Nothing is sketchy, pencil-like or hand-lettered. Two are animated GIFs of the decoding loop; the rest are static PNGs. Second drift: the claim implies a current explainer, but the page is the unmodified June 2018 text describing the original encoder-decoder Transformer, and Alammar's own banner directs readers wanting current architectures (Multi-Query Attention, RoPE) to Chapter 3 of his book instead. Third: nothing on the page is interactive — no sliders, no runnable attention viewer. The one "interactive visualization" it points to is an external Tensor2Tensor Colab notebook, and that repo is archived by Google (last push 2023-06-02).

claimsInaccurate.name: AttentionViz
claimsInaccurate.correction: Two problems. First, the site does not currently do the thing at all: the frontend on GitHub Pages is HTTPS-only (HSTS enforced) but hard-codes its data API as plain http:// to a bare EC2 IP with no TLS, so every browser blocks the fetch as mixed content and the app hangs on "Loading..." permanently. You see the controls, never a single attention plot. Second, even when working the claim mis-describes the mechanism. It does not show "attention patterns" as attention-weight heatmaps in the usual sense — the core view is a scatterplot of a joint t-SNE/UMAP/PCA projection of the query and key VECTORS, where proximity is a proxy for attention weight. Attention-weight rendering (BertViz-style lines, heatmaps) only appears in the drill-down Sentence/Image view. Third, "real transformer models" is three fixed pre-computed models — BERT, GPT-2, ViT — not a model you choose or supply; and the app boots on the vision transformer (vit-nat), not a language model. The sequences are a fixed pre-computed corpus per model; you cannot enter your own text or upload an image.

claimsInaccurate.name: ConvNet Playground
claimsInaccurate.correction: The first clause is right (and understated — it is 9 models in search, 11 in the explorer, not 3). The second clause, "see which neurons activate for which patterns," inverts the actual mechanism. There is no activation view: you cannot feed an input and watch neurons light up, and you cannot upload an image anywhere in the app. The Model Explorer shows optimization-based feature visualization via the Lucid library — synthetic images grown from random noise by gradient ascent to *maximally excite* a channel. That is the opposite direction: "what synthetic input would most excite this channel", not "which neurons fired for this pattern". Three further overstatements: it is channels (groups of neurons), never individual neurons; only 30 randomly selected channels per layer are shown, as precomputed static JPEGs you cannot choose or re-run; and non-differentiable layers are skipped entirely. The whole app is precomputed — the FAQ states it flatly — so nothing is "extracted" at your request; you are browsing a lookup table over 4 datasets x 200 images x 9 models x 8 layers x 4 distance metrics. Also note the app's real centrepiece, semantic image search with a rank-weighted retrieval score, does not appear in the PDF claim at all.

claimsInaccurate.name: Image Kernels Explained
claimsInaccurate.correction: The filters half is right — outline, blur, sharpen are all there, plus emboss, identity and four Sobels (nine kernels, all fixed at 3x3). "Drag-and-drop" is simply wrong: there is no drag-and-drop interaction anywhere on the page. You pick a kernel from an HTML dropdown, and you build a custom kernel by typing numbers into nine spinner inputs (range -10 to 10, step 0.1). Swapping in your own picture is a plain file-picker <input type="file">, not a drop zone — I grepped script.js for drop/dragover handlers and there are none. Also worth flagging for the "CNNs & CV" category: this page teaches the convolution operation only. It never touches learned filters, backprop, channels/depth (grayscale single-channel throughout), stride, dilation, pooling, activations, or layer stacking. Kernel size is hard-coded 3x3 with no way to try 5x5 or 1x1, and padding is described in prose but is not adjustable.

claimsInaccurate.name: Distill.pub
claimsInaccurate.correction: Two errors. (1) There is no AutoML content on Distill — not one article, not one mention. The archive grep for "automl" and "architecture search" returns nothing across all 45+ articles from 2016 to 2021. The nearest thing is "Exploring Bayesian Optimization" (Agnihotri & Batra, May 5 2020), which teaches GP surrogates and acquisition functions for hyperparameter search — adjacent to AutoML but not AutoML or neural architecture search. Whoever wrote the PDF line appears to have pattern-matched a generic "ML topics" list. (2) The claim is phrased in the present tense as if Distill is a live journal. It is not. It has been on indefinite hiatus since July 2, 2021, publishes nothing new, and explicitly no longer accepts submissions. It is a frozen archive — an excellent one, but a museum, not a publication. The accurate parts: "research articles with interactive visualizations" and "how neural networks see, feature visualization" are correct and are in fact the site's strongest material (Feature Visualization 2017, The Building Blocks of Interpretability 2018, Activation Atlas 2019, and the entire Circuits thread 2020-21).

claimsInaccurate.name: Gradient Descent Visualizer
claimsInaccurate.correction: The first clause is right, the second is fabricated. There IS a gradient-descent-on-a-contour-plot demo with an adjustable learning rate, so "watch gradient descent crawl across a loss landscape" holds. But the page contains NO SGD, NO momentum, and NO Adam — I grepped the full HTML for Adam/momentum/SGD/RMSprop/Adagrad and got zero hits. The three algorithms it actually implements and compares are Nelder-Mead (derivative-free simplex), plain full-batch Gradient Descent (with an optional Wolfe line-search checkbox), and Non-Linear Conjugate Gradient (Polak-Ribiere). So the comparison axis is derivative-free vs first-order vs curvature-aware classical optimization — NOT the deep-learning adaptive-optimizer axis the PDF promises. The descent is deterministic full-gradient on 2-D closed-form test functions (Himmelblau, Rosenbrock, x^2+y^2+x sin y+y sin x, .26(x^2+y^2)+.48xy); there is no minibatch, no noise, no stochasticity anywhere. Pointedly, the page's Further Reading section sends you AWAY to Sebastian Ruder's overview for stochastic gradient descent — the author explicitly scoped SGD out. A learner arriving to "compare SGD, momentum, Adam" will find none of the three.

claimsInaccurate.name: ML Playground
claimsInaccurate.correction: The five algorithms named are exactly right (KNN, Perceptron, SVM, Artificial Neural Network, Decision Tree), but two parts of the claim have drifted. (1) There is no drag-and-drop. You place points by single-clicking the canvas — the tour's first step literally says "Click to add data points" — and you cannot drag a placed point to move it. The only file affordance is a plain "Upload Data" file-picker input alongside "Save Data"; it is not a drop zone. (2) "Watch ... draw decision boundaries" overstates the interactivity. Training is not animated. You press Train, the button turns black and blocks, and a finished boundary appears all at once. There is no epoch-by-epoch animation, no loss curve, no weight or per-neuron output display. The tour itself warns: "some models can take time to train (sometimes up to 10-20 seconds). If the button remains black, chances are it's still training." Anyone expecting TensorFlow Playground's live training dynamics will be disappointed. Separately, only two classes plus an eraser exist, so the "Multi-class Classification" and "Regression" use cases that each model's own write-up lists cannot actually be exercised — the tool is binary 2D classification only.

claimsInaccurate.name: DBSCAN Visualization (Naftali Harris)
claimsInaccurate.correction: The first half is accurate — it is a real, still-running density-based clustering visualization. The second half is overstated. The page contains no k-means comparison at all: no side-by-side, no k-means run, no overlay. It has one closing sentence linking to Harris's separate k-means post and asking the reader to go run the same datasets there and judge for themselves. So "why DBSCAN handles shapes K-means can't" is a conclusion you must assemble yourself across two pages, and even then the page never states the reason — it never mentions convexity, Voronoi partitions, or centroid geometry as the mechanism behind k-means's failure on rings. It demonstrates the what, never the why. Two smaller drifts: the datasets are not free-form "shapes" — they are eight fixed generators with no upload, no click-to-place points, and no two-moons; and the epsilon slider is hard-capped at 2.0 with minPoints capped at 6, so the parameter space you can explore is narrow.

claimsInaccurate.name: Diffusion Explainer (Polo Club)
claimsInaccurate.correction: Directionally right but overstates the interactivity in two specific ways. (1) You cannot enter your own prompt. "Select another prompt" opens a picker of 13 hard-coded prompt pairs (bunny/pixar, cityscape, spiderman in space, Kinkade vs Van Gogh, etc.). There is no text input anywhere on the page. (2) Guidance scale is not an adjustable slider — it is a dropdown with exactly four precomputed values: 0.0, 1.0, 7.0, 20.0. Seed is likewise a 3-option dropdown (1, 2, 3) and timesteps are fixed at 50. Nothing is computed in the browser: every frame is a pre-rendered JPG at assets/img/{prompt}/{seed}_{gs}_{timestep}.jpg, so the combinatorial space you can explore is 13 prompt-pairs x 3 seeds x 4 guidance values. The "step by step" part of the claim is fully accurate — the timestep slider with play/pause/step-forward/step-back genuinely scrubs all 50 refinement steps and shows both the latent visualization and the decoded image at each one.

claimsInaccurate.name: Embedding Projector (TensorFlow)
claimsInaccurate.correction: Two of the three clauses hold; the GloVe clause is wrong. "Visualize high-dimensional embeddings in 3D" is accurate (PCA, t-SNE and UMAP each have a 2D/3D toggle, defaulting to 3D). "Load Word2Vec" is accurate — two Word2Vec sets ship built in: "Word2Vec 10K" (10000x200) and "Word2Vec All" (71291x200). But there is no GloVe dataset anywhere on the site. The complete built-in list is Word2Vec 10K, Word2Vec All, "Mnist with images" (10000x784 with a sprite sheet), Iris (150x4), and "GNMT Interlingua" (9978x1024). The strings "GloVe" and "glove" appear zero times in the 1.86 MB bundle and zero times in the demo config. You can load GloVe only by downloading it yourself and uploading it as a tab-separated vectors file via the Load panel ("Step 1: Load a TSV file of vectors") — there is no GloVe preset or one-click load. The claim also undersells the tool: beyond "see clustering" it does nearest-neighbor retrieval (cosine or Euclidean, in either original or projected space), regex search, isolate-selection filtering, L2 normalization via "Sphereize data", supervised t-SNE, and custom user-defined semantic axes.

claimsInaccurate.name: REINFORCEjs Gridworld (Karpathy)
claimsInaccurate.correction: Q-learning and SARSA are real and switchable; policy gradients are not on this page at all. The spec textarea exposes exactly two update rules — `spec.update = 'qlearn'` or `'sarsa'` — and nothing else. No policy-gradient demo exists anywhere in the REINFORCEjs suite: the nav is About / GridWorld: DP / GridWorld: TD / PuckWorld: DQN / WaterWorld: DQN, and I confirmed all four pages return 200 with no PG page among them. The rl.js library does define SimpleReinforceAgent and RecurrentReinforceAgent, but they are not wired to any demo page, and Karpathy's own README labels them "very alpha, likely buggy or at the very least finicky and inconsistent". The page source even carries a commented-out `//agent = new RL.ActorCriticAgent(env, {...})` line — and grepping rl.js shows the only agent classes are DPAgent, TDAgent, DQNAgent, SimpleReinforceAgent, RecurrentReinforceAgent, so no ActorCriticAgent class exists and uncommenting it would throw. Second overstatement: this demo is fully tabular (100 discrete states, a flat Q array), no neural network anywhere — the "deep" RL in this suite lives on the separate PuckWorld/WaterWorld DQN pages. Third: the PDF says "watch an agent learn to navigate a gridworld," which undersells the actual differentiator — the planning (Dyna) and prioritized-sweeping knobs, which is the part of this page you cannot get from a textbook.

claimsInaccurate.name: Netron (Model Architecture Viewer)
claimsInaccurate.correction: Three corrections. (1) ".pth" is the weak link and the most common disappointment: a plain PyTorch state_dict .pth does NOT render as an architecture graph. In source/pytorch.js the loader falls back to `pytorch.Utility.weights(module)` and emits one node of type 'Weights' per parameter tensor (lines ~280-290) — you get a disconnected inventory of parameter names, dtypes and shapes with no operators and no data flow. To see actual PyTorch architecture you must first export to TorchScript (torch.jit.trace/script → .pt), torch.export, ExecuTorch, or ONNX. Same weight-list-only behaviour applies to Safetensors, GGUF and NumPy files, which are weight containers with no graph. (2) "Upload" is wrong in the user's favour: nothing is uploaded. The file is read via the File API and parsed in a browser worker; netron.app is a static site with no backend, so it is safe for proprietary models. (3) "any model file" undersells and overpromises at once — the real list is far longer than four (ONNX, TFLite, PyTorch, torch.export, ExecuTorch, TorchScript, TensorFlow, Core ML, OpenVINO, Keras, Caffe, Darknet, Safetensors, NumPy; experimental MLIR, JAX, GGUF, RKNN, ncnn, MNN, PaddlePaddle, scikit-learn) but it is a read-only structural viewer: no inference, no activation values, no editing, no profiling, no latency data.

challengeVerdicts.name: TensorFlow Playground
challengeVerdicts.why:
n = number of proposed matches audited (no batch index was supplied in the prompt).

WHAT SURVIVES. All five named subtopics exist verbatim in /tmp/ml-topics.json — I string-matched each. The gap claim also survives: grepping all 827 subtopic strings for boundary/expressiv/universal/hidden layer/hidden unit/half-plane/approximat/depth/width/piecewise/perceptron returns only "Expressive power: 1-WL, GIN..." (row 119, GNN-specific), "Impurity criteria and the piecewise-constant geometry of a tree" (102), "Maximum-margin geometry..." and "k-NN... the Voronoi boundary" (103). Zero hits for universal approximation, hidden layer, hidden unit, half-plane, or perceptron anywhere. Track O is complete in the file (rows 111–119), so the scope is real. The gap is correctly claimed, and match 4 (row 105) is a correct, well-evidenced negative — row 105 does contain "Target encoding: deriving the empirical-Bayes shrinkage estimator", "Filter selection: mutual information...", "Permutation importance and the correlated-feature trap", "Metrics that survive a 1 percent base rate", "Resampling inside the fold", with Lemaitre/Kaggle FE as watch/do exactly as described.

WHY IT IS STILL REFUTED — match 1 (row 111, rated "strong") is padded on two of its three subtopics, and it is the entry doing the most work in the bundle.

1. "L2 / weight decay: the shrinkage update and where it must not apply" is a vocabulary collision, not a teaching match. The subtopic names two things: the shrinkage form of the update (w ← w − ηλw) and the parameter groups decay must be excluded from (biases, norm scale/shift — cf. row 112's "AdamW: decoupled weight decay and the no-decay parameter group"). Playground exposes no update rule, no numeric weights, no biases as separable parameters, and has no normalisation layers at all. A slider labelled "L2" plus a rate is the entire overlap. This is precisely the "attention in a 3D GPT walkthrough" failure the audit warns about.

2. The stated headline value of match 1 — "an L1-vs-L2 contrast where L1 visibly deletes connections from the diagram while L2 only thins them" — maps to nothing in row 111. Grepping "L1" across all 827 returns only row 105 ("Embedded and wrapper selection: L1 paths..."); row 111's regularisation subtopics are L2/weight decay, dropout, and early stopping only. The L1-sparsity payload belongs to row 101 (Lasso subgradients/soft-thresholding/coefficient path), where the proposal itself concedes StatQuest already covers it and explicitly disclaims it as a reason to send him there. So the single most vivid thing Playground offers is homeless in both rows it is pitched at.

3. "Activation functions and their derivatives: saturation and dead units" — Playground renders no derivatives anywhere. It covers the back half (saturation, dead units) via neuron tiles; the front half is absent, which is the half the row's depth target actually needs.

4. Row 111's topic title includes "initialisation" and its subtopics include the Xavier and Kaiming variance derivations. Playground has no initialisation control of any kind. The proposal does not flag this, while still awarding "strong".

Net: of row 111's 20 subtopics, Playground partially touches roughly 1.5, cannot touch the depth target by the proposal's own admission ("no gradient, no weight update, no backprop maths is exposed anywhere"), and one of the three claimed subtopics is name-only. A reviewer looking to cut would cut this entry, or downgrade it to "weak / optional". "Strong" is overstated, and the bundle as presented should not ship unchanged.

Two smaller notes. Match 2 misses a better home the proposal never considers: row 95 (Calculus and optimisation) contains "Reading a bad loss curve: an ordered diagnostic", which is a closer fit than row 112's "Loss-curve taxonomy" and whose existing do (D2L ch.12 from-scratch optimisers) leaves the same generator-shaped hole. Match 2 also slightly overstates the noise claim — label noise floors *test* loss; with enough capacity training loss still drops through it, which is the opposite of "no matter how much capacity you add".

challengeVerdicts.name: ML Visualized
challengeVerdicts.why:
n = 1 of 5 proposed matches survives. No subtopic name is hallucinated — all 11 verify verbatim in /tmp/ml-topics.json. But three of five matches, including the flagship "exact", claim teaching the site does not do, and the gap claim is a vocabulary artifact.

ROW 111 ("exact") — REFUTED, and it is the worst of the five. The core claim ("writes out the full chain-rule expansion of dJ/dW1, dJ/dW2, dJ/dW3") is false. chapter4/neural_network.html derives ONLY the last layer and says so in its own words: "Let's derive a general formula to update the weight matrix W_i and bias vector B_i of a single fully-connected layer." Every expansion is written for W3/B3. dJ/dW1 and dJ/dW2 are named once in a list of goals and never expanded; the recursion — the actual content of "Hand-deriving the backward pass of an L-layer MLP" — is disposed of in prose: "In the general case for any layer, this is the gradient from the next layer (idx+1)." No transposes, no W_{i+1}^T delta_{i+1}, no shape discipline; it even writes dA_3/dB_3 mid-derivation as a typo. "Jacobian" = 0 hits across all 12 notebooks, so "Vanishing and exploding gradients as a product of Jacobians" is vocabulary overlap only — the Vanishing Gradients section is four sentences of prose plus a PyTorch training log, with no product expression, no per-layer gradient norms, and "exploding" = 0 hits. Row 111's depth statement demands a finite-difference check to ~1e-7: "gradient check", "finite difference", "numerical gradient", "1e-7" = 0 hits site-wide, while CS231n ships eval_numerical_gradient and does exactly that. Row 111's title also covers initialisation and regularisation: "dropout" 0, "regulari*" 0, "weight decay" 0, "BatchNorm" 0, "Kaiming" 0, "GELU" 0, "Xavier" = one code comment. Finally the differentiator argument is factually wrong: CS231n does ship the derivation (cs231n.github.io/optimization-2 has a "Gradients for vectorized operations" section, and the course's linked linear-layer handout is more rigorous than the site's).

ROW 95 ("strong") — REFUTED as padding. Three of four named subtopics are untaught. "Nesterov" 0 hits, "AdaGrad" 0 hits site-wide; there is no momentum optimizer at all — the page implements exactly SGD (params - lr*grad, no velocity), RMSprop and Adam, and "momentum" appears only as a descriptive phrase inside the Adam prose. "Rosenbrock" 0, "ill-condition" 0, "log scale" 0, so "Benchmarking optimisers honestly: Rosenbrock, ill-conditioned quadratics, and log-scale plots" is flatly false. "Adam: derive the bias correction" — the page states the formula with a one-clause justification, it does not derive it. The stated differentiator also collapses: d2l 12.1 already plots the identical surface, z = x**2 - y**2, as a 3D saddle wireframe, and d2l 12.6-12.11 implement Momentum, Adagrad, RMSProp, Adadelta, Adam and LR scheduling from scratch. The site adds animation to a figure the existing `do` already draws, while covering strictly less.

ROW 101 ("strong") — REFUTED. The model is scalar y = wx + b: "normal equation" 0, "design matrix" 0, "step size" 0, "condition" 0, so two of the three components of "Gradient descent for OLS: the update rule, the step-size bound, and conditioning" are absent. "Hessian" 0, "IRLS" 0, "ridge"/"lasso"/"bias-variance" 0. The interactivity claim is unverified: the three "interactive" pages are bare iframes to third-party marimo.app permalinks with show-code=false and literally zero prose on the page; "slider" and "paraboloid" appear nowhere on the site, so "dragging w and b on the 3D MSE paraboloid" is inferred, not observed. Worst, the Bernoulli-likelihood-and-gradient content credited here is the same chapter3/logistic_regression.html notebook that is the entire basis of the row 99 match — the same page is billed twice.

ROW 107 ("strong") — survives only at reduced strength; "strong" is overstated. The Lagrange-multiplier derivation is genuinely on the page (constraint v^T v = 1, Lagrangian, (x^T x)v = lambda v) and it is checked against scikit-learn, and neither StatQuest nor ISLP Ch12 derives it. But "SVD" 0, "Eckart" 0, "scree" 0, so it delivers one of the three items in its own named subtopic, the algebra is loose (it asserts x^T x "is the covariance" without centring/normalisation), and row 94 already carries "PCA done properly", "Eckart-Young-Mirsky" and the spectral theorem with the fast.ai notebooks. Net marginal value: one derivation. Downgrade to weak, keep only if a one-subtopic add is worth a row entry.

GAP CLAIM — REFUTED. The greps are literally true (autoencoder/manifold/reconstruct/warp = 0 across 43 topics, 43 depth statements, 827 subtopics; "latent" only row 110's matrix-factorisation factors — I reproduced all of these), but the inference does not follow. Representation geometry has four named homes: row 107 "PCA when the matrix is large or the structure is nonlinear" (the kernel-PCA/autoencoder slot) plus "Measuring what an embedding destroyed: trustworthiness, continuity and stability"; row 118 "The dual-encoder contract: what a 'shared embedding space' actually is", "L2 normalisation, cosine similarity, and the alignment/uniformity decomposition", "The modality gap: two cones, not one sphere", "Projection heads, and why the best features are the ones you throw away"; row 94 "Embedding matrices: cosine, normalisation, anisotropy and collapse" and "Low-rank structure in deep learning: LoRA, bottlenecks and attention shapes"; row 116 "The residual stream and the shape contract of a decoder block" and "QK and OV circuits: what the four projection matrices actually parameterise". That is learned-latent-space geometry taught more rigorously than a GIF of layer warping. This is a lexical gap, not a curricular one — and the proposal concedes the site cannot fill it anyway, which makes it a recommendation to open a hole rather than close one.

challengeVerdicts.name: Gradient Descent Visualizer
challengeVerdicts.why:

Divergence is reachable only on Himmelblau (eta=0.05 blows up at iter 6), a non-convex quartic with no fixed lambda_max — the wrong object for a bound defined by a quadratic's spectrum. REFUTATION 2 — subtopic B is vocabulary overlap, not teaching. The site's entire treatment of the dual encoder is three sentences (text_l3expl.js: the text encoder makes a vector "close to the image's vector, produced by a paired image encoder (not used in Stable Diffusion), in hybrid text-image space") plus a static three-label diagram, and one prose sentence in description.js. Zero occurrences of "cosine", "contrast", "similarit" (as a computed quantity), "pool", or "normalis" across description.js / text_l2expl.js / text_l3expl.js. The site ASSERTS the shared space in one sentence and immediately parenthesises the image half as unused — precisely the failure mode the proposal claims it fixes ("concrete rather than asserted"). Worse, the mechanism it actually demonstrates — a text vector steering generation — is cross-attention conditioning. Stable Diffusion never compares a text vector to an image vector, so watching a prompt steer a trajectory demonstrates that the vector carries semantics, not that it lives in a space shared with image embeddings. Category error.

REFUTATION 3 — whatItAdds is false against the row's existing DO. The claim "it gives something no plan resource gives: a downstream consumer of a CLIP text vector" is contradicted by row 118's own do (moein-shariatnia/OpenAI-CLIP), which trains a dual encoder and then "query it with text to retrieve images" — a downstream consumer where the shared-space property is actually load-bearing. That repo also already covers the padding/truncation mechanic in runnable code (`tokenizer(..., padding=True, truncation=True, max_length=CFG.max_length)`) and teaches "which vector you pool" explicitly and with reasoning (README: "To grab the whole representation of a sentence ... we use the final representations of the CLS token"). Diffusion Explainer covers pooling not at all — SD consumes all 77 vectors, so a learner takes away the wrong mental model for exactly the clause the existing do gets right.

NET: after stripping the false UI claim, the site's unique contribution to row 118 is one paragraph stating the constant 77, whose justification is a hand-wave ("to balance performance and computational efficiency"). That is a number, not a mechanism, bought for 25 minutes of a 13.5-hour row, in a wrapper that teaches token==word and models the CLIP interface incorrectly for retrieval. "strength: strong" is unsupportable; even "weak" is generous. A reviewer wanting to cut this would cut it.

GAP CLAIM — CONFIRMED, accurate, keep it. Independently grepped all 43 topics / 827 subtopics plus every topic, depth, watch and do label: zero hits for diffusion, denois*, unet, u-net, vae, autoencoder, guidance, classifier-free, text-to-image, flow matching, score-based. The only "latent" hits are row 110's matrix-factorisation subtopic, its depth line and its watch label — exactly as claimed. The only generative-model hit is row 99's "JS divergence, f-divergences, and what a GAN is actually minimising" — exactly as claimed. Track O runs 111 (NN foundations) to 119 (GNNs) and contains no generative-modelling row. The proposer's self-limiting judgement (genuine gap, but the site cannot fill it — inference-only, no forward noising process, no training objective, frozen at SD v1.x) is correct and appropriately cautious. Forward the gap; drop the match. If the parent wants image generation in the plan it needs its own row, and even then this site is a 25-minute visual aside, not the spine.

challengeVerdicts.name: Embedding Projector (TensorFlow)
challengeVerdicts.why:
Mixed, but refuted as submitted: one row rests on a fabricated tool feature, one row is self-confessed padding with an affirmative technical error, and only row 107 survives — and only after striking a subtopic.

WHAT CHECKS OUT. All 9 named subtopics exist verbatim (exact string match, no paraphrase): row 107 #17/#18/#19/#15/#2, row 94 #18/#15, row 118 #12/#4. Plan really is 43 topics / 827 subtopics. Row 107's DO (ISLP Ch12, USArrests+NCI60) genuinely has no t-SNE and no UMAP, and its WATCH names only "PCA Step-by-Step, t-SNE, Hierarchical Clustering, K-means, DBSCAN" — no UMAP. I fetched https://projector.tensorflow.org/oss_data/oss_demo_projector_config.json: the five datasets and shapes are exactly as described (10000x200, 71291x200, MNIST 10000x784 + sprite, Iris 150x4, GNMT 9978x1024). I grepped the shipped 1.8MB bundle and confirmed in code: perplexity tooltip ("5 to 50"), learning-rate tooltip, Supervise slider 0-100, UMAP nNeighbors default 15, Run/Pause/Perturb buttons + Iteration counter, PCA sampling notice, COSINE/EUCLIDEAN toggle, and the CUSTOM tab computing sub(centroids.xRight, centroids.xLeft) then projectLinear — a literal centroid-difference axis.

FATAL DEFECT, ROW 107. The load-bearing justification for "Measuring what an embedding destroyed: trustworthiness, continuity and stability" is a hallucinated feature. The claim is "a separate 'nearest neighbours in original space vs in the projection' setting". The app has exactly ONE knn path: DataSet.findNeighbors = knn.findKNNofPoint(this.points, h, l, function(m){return m.vector}, k) — always the original high-dimensional vector. I grepped every findKNN* call site; all use point.vector, and there are ZERO knn calls over point.projections[...]. The two tooltips ("in the original space" / "in the selected space") are duplicated sliders in vz-projector-inspector-panel: the first sits above the "Nearest points in the original space:" list; the second sits inside the .metadata-info panel above "{{metadataColumn}} labels (click to apply):" — the metadata-labelling UI — and BOTH bind the same numNN property with the same updateNumNN handler. A tooltip was misread into a feature, and the same fabrication is in the parent's Concepts list ("exposed as two separate settings"). Strike subtopic 19: trustworthiness and continuity are quantitative metrics this tool never computes; only the "stability" third is salvageable via Perturb (verified: tsne.perturb() jitters Y by 0.1*maxradius). Two further precision errors: UMAP_SAMPLE_SIZE=5E3, so UMAP runs on a 5,000-point subsample, not the 10,000x200 matrix; and PCA is truncated to 10 components, so the "scree plot" lesson is a 10-bar stub.

ROW 94 OVERSTATED. "Sphereize" is not L2 normalisation — DataSet.normalize() subtracts the GLOBAL CENTROID and then unit-normalises (tooltip confirms). It does mutate point.vector, so "watch the neighbour list change" is true, and the cosine/euclidean toggle does re-run findNeighbors. But 2 of the subtopic's 4 words (anisotropy, collapse) get nothing (admitted), the topic's depth statement is entirely hand-derived SVD / condition number / rank which the tool never touches, and the PCA-variance value is the same value already claimed at row 107 — one toy billed twice. "strong" is not defensible; weak-and-optional at best.

ROW 118 REFUTED OUTRIGHT. It concedes "Out of the box: nothing" and volunteers to be dropped. Worse, its one concrete manipulation is wrong: CLIP embeddings are already L2-normalised and already on the unit sphere, so "Sphereize data making the unit-sphere framing literal" is backwards — sphereize subtracts the global centroid (which for image+text pairs sits BETWEEN the two cones) before renormalising, altering precisely the origin-relative geometry that "two cones, not one sphere" is about. And the proposal is not a resource: it is "export TSVs from the DO you already have," which matplotlib does in five lines.

GAP CLAIM: UPHELD, and it is the strongest part of the submission. I grepped topic, depth, watch label, do label and all 827 subtopics independently: 'analogy' 0, 'fairness' 0, 'word2vec' 0, 'semantic direction' 0, 'centroid' 0, 'concept' 0, 'steer' 0, 'gender' 0, 'demograph' 0, 'ethic' 0. 'bias' is 22 hits and every one is bias-variance, Adam bias correction, estimator bias, exposure bias, popularity bias, model-selection bias, inductive bias, or length bias — exactly as stated. The only 'probe' is r118 "Adapting to a customer: zero-shot, linear probe...". I also checked r108 (Explainability) directly: SHAP/LIME/PDP/ICE/ALE/Shapley/counterfactuals — feature attribution on tabular models, nothing about directions in an embedding space. The gap is real.

The demo never instantiates offline learning at all, so it structurally cannot show the distinction "when online RLHF still wins" is trading on.
3. The lesson points backwards. The tutorial's own stated conclusion is that Q-Learning "converges much faster than SARSA" on this exact gridworld — i.e. off-policy wins. The subtopic asserts online/on-policy still wins. A learner transferring the analogy to the nearest-sounding pair (DPO=offline, PPO=online) draws the opposite conclusion. Actively misleading, not scaffolding.
4. Existing resources already cover it. The row's watch label states verbatim that CS336 L15 covers "instruction tuning data, reward models, Bradley-Terry, PPO vs DPO, length bias." The row's depth statement's only RL-side bar is "derive the DPO loss from the Bradley-Terry model well enough to say what beta does" plus reading rewards/margins, rewards/accuracies and win-rate. Nothing in it requires TD learning, value functions, eligibility traces, Dyna or prioritised sweeping. The page's distinguishing knobs (planN, prioritised sweeping) — which the gap claim itself calls the part "you genuinely cannot get from a textbook" — are 100% irrelevant to row 117. Padding.
5. Self-defeating caveat. The proposal says send Rasul to "the demo panel and the prose, not the derivations," but the SARSA-vs-Q-learning contrast IS a derivation in the prose. Spending 25 min of a 16-hour, 20-subtopic row on a degraded page teaching the wrong axis does not survive a reviewer who wants to cut.

GAP CLAIM: substantively CONFIRMED, with two corrections. No topic title is RL. Row 98 confirmed to contain mSPRT and alpha spending and no explore/exploit allocation. False friends verified. CORRECTION B: scope overreach — the file's 43 topics are rows 50-66 and 94-119, a filtered ML/AI extract; rows 1-49 and 67-93 are absent, so "absent from the entire plan" is asserted on 43 of ~119 rows. challengeVerdicts.name: Netron (Model Architecture Viewer)
challengeVerdicts.why:
VERIFIED CLEAN — subtopic strings and the gap. All 13 named subtopics exist verbatim in /tmp/ml-topics.json (checked by exact string match against rows 111/113/114/116/117; note rowIndex = the file's `index`, row = `row`). Counts check out: 43 topics, 827 subtopics. The claimed GAP is REAL and correctly stated: across every topic, depth, watch label, do label and all 827 subtopics, the strings onnx, torchscript, torch.export, torch.jit, executorch, tflite, coreml/core ml, openvino, serialis/serializ, export, convert, package, interop, on-device, mobile all return ZERO hits. deploy/compile return exactly 5 hits (row 52 "Ship it: stateless deploy", row 57 x3 Hermes container, row 116 torch.compile) — the write-up says "four", a trivial miscount that does not touch the substance. The nearest adjacent coverage is genuinely not the same thing: row 55 "The adapter artefact: what you are actually shipping" / "Serving: merged weights versus runtime adapters" is LLM-adapter-specific, row 62 is entirely vLLM-server-side, row 63 is registries/rollout. Do not cut the gap. The proposer's own caveat (Netron reads such an artifact, it cannot produce one) is correct and honest.

WHY THE MAPPING IS STILL REFUTED — the matches themselves are overstated, three of the four actively so.

Row 113 (PyTorch at depth, claimed "strong") — cut it. The entire pitch is built on a Netron *limitation* (a .pth state_dict renders as a flat weight list, not a graph). The lesson delivered — "a checkpoint is a flat dict of named tensors" — is one line of Python (`sd.keys()`, `v.dtype`, `v.shape`) and Netron renders it strictly worse than `print`. Half the named subtopic is invisible to the tool: hooks and train/eval have no Netron representation at all. The second subtopic is misread: it says "the precision budget you are actually training in", and the pitch answers "confirm what precision your checkpoint was actually saved in" — under AMP those differ (autocast trains in bf16/fp16 against fp32 master weights that get saved as fp32), so the tool tells you the opposite of what the subtopic asks. Netron also has no concept of `device`. Vocabulary overlap, not teaching.

Row 117 (Fine-tuning at depth, claimed "strong") — cut to at most one subtopic, and it is marginal. "LoRA: the maths you must be able to write from memory" is not taught: you see two matrices of compatible shape; the product, the alpha/r scaling and the merge are not shown, so "W + BA verified by inspection" is false. "Choosing r, lora_alpha, target_modules, dropout and the learning rate" — lora_alpha, dropout and LR live in adapter_config.json, which Netron does not render, so 3 of the 5 named knobs are invisible, and the subtopic is about *choosing*, not reading off. Only "PEFT mechanics and shipping the adapter" is a real fit, and row 55 already carries "The adapter artefact: what you are actually shipping" plus "PEFT wiring: wrap, verify, save, hot-swap". Also evidentiary: safetensors is not among the formats attested in the supplied resource description, and the pitch itself concedes you should "use the pip/desktop build, not netron.app" — i.e. not the resource being mapped.

Row 116 (Transformers from scratch, claimed "strong") — cut it. It is circular: the whole match presupposes the learner can export a GPT-2/DistilBERT to ONNX, which is precisely the skill the same submission proves the plan never teaches. It duplicates the existing pair in a worse form: Karpathy's "Let's build GPT" spends minutes on `.view(B,T,nh,hs).transpose(1,2)` and the Annotated Transformer is a runnable notebook where any shape is one `print(x.shape)` away — a noisy 200-node ONNX graph is a harder way to see the same thing, as the proposal's own "visually noisy, 15-minute look" caveat concedes. The resource's attested concept list is CNN-centric (SqueezeNet, MobileNet, BatchNorm, TFLite); the transformer use is the proposer's extrapolation.

Row 114 (Computer vision, claimed "exact") — survives, but not at "exact", and one load-bearing claim is false. "Nothing in the current pair gives a per-layer, shape-annotated view of a real trained net" is wrong: the CS231n CNN-architectures lecture in the mapped Spring 2025 playlist is famous for exactly that — the AlexNet/VGG table of per-layer output volume, memory and parameter count. Two of the five subtopics are vocabulary-only. "EfficientNet: compound scaling, MBConv, and what the FLOP count hides" — compound scaling is invisible in a single graph and "what the FLOP count hides" (latency, memory traffic) is not shown at all; the pitch also conflates MobileNetV1's depthwise-separable pair with MBConv, which is the inverted-residual-plus-SE block, not the same thing. "Batch normalisation: the exact computation, train vs eval, and where it breaks" — seeing four stored tensors is evidence consistent with the asymmetry for someone who already knows it, not a teaching of it; and ONNX export folds BN into the preceding Conv by default, so on a stock ResNet ONNX those four tensors are usually not there (the resource's own example is TF/Keras-named). "Building ResNet-18 by hand" is partial: a stock torchvision ResNet-18 shows the ImageNet 7x7-stride-2 stem, i.e. the opposite of the named CIFAR stem.

Row 111 (self-ruled-out) — the "do not slot it here" call is correct: Netron has no gradients and no backward pass, and micrograd already draws the graph with grads on every node.

Net: one defensible slot, narrowed. A reviewer looking to cut has three easy kills and a demonstrably false "nothing in the current pair" claim in the fourth.
